Unreachable branch. This is the else of the receive handler's four-way branch (lines 47-55): it runs only when NWConnection reports no content, no error and isComplete false. Over a stream connection asked for minimumIncompleteLength 1 that combination does not occur - no content always arrives with isComplete or an error, both handled above. Probed with 250 receives (200 racing close(), 50 racing peer EOF, plus receives after EOF and before open): every one reported bytes, isComplete, or a transport error, never empty content, so no test can reach the deleted statement.

Proven equivalent, because of the close on the next line. The reader task suspends in exactly three places, all of them SocketConnection calls - open (line 44), send (line 45) and the receive inside pumpFrames (line 99); everything between them is synchronous, and AsyncThrowingStream.yield never suspends. connection.close() at line 40 cancels the NWConnection, and a cancelled connection ends every one of those calls: SocketConnectionTests.testSendFailsOnceTheConnectionIsClosed, testReceiveFailsOnceTheConnectionIsClosed and testAFailedOpenLeavesNothingDialling pin that. Proven equivalent, empirically. `init` sets every stored property (client, authorizer, presenter) and then calls `super.init()`; with that call deleted by hand, `swift build` produces zero errors and zero warnings, and the whole ThrowntomUITests target (539 tests) still passes byte-for-byte identically. Swift's two-phase initializer rule ordinarily requires an explicit delegating call before an initializer returns, but for a designated initializer whose superclass (NSObject here) has a no-argument initializer, the compiler synthesizes that call itself when the source omits it -- there is nothing left for the deleted statement to do that the compiler was not already going to do. No test can distinguish the two forms because the compiled program is the same program either way.
